scope: Seven Lanslots historical/biblical over-inferences flagged during nonparenthetical verse association. These are substantive critical source readings, not blanket denials of Catholic liturgical doctrine.

When the people of Israel, after a long and dreary journey in the desert, had reached the Land of Promise, after they had ended their wanderings, and had now perma- nently set up their tents, they erected a mag- nificent altar in the Temple of Jerusalem. This wonder of art, on which neither gold nor silver
records.lanslotsOriginalArgument: Lanslots groups Abel, Noe and Abraham among patriarchs who erected altars. Genesis 8:20 explicitly mentions Noe building an altar; Genesis 4:4 records Abel's offering but not a built altar.
records.criticalEnglishAssessment: Abel's offering is recorded in Scripture, but unlike Noe's sacrifice the text does not explicitly describe him constructing an altar. Their offerings may prefigure Christ without proving the physical continuity of every altar.
records.substantiveFrenchResearchDraft: Le récit biblique rapporte l'offrande d'Abel sans dire expressément qu'il construisit un autel; il décrit en revanche l'autel dressé par Noé. La figure du Sacrifice ne constitue pas une démonstration d'identité historique des cérémonies.

records.lanslotsOriginalArgument: Lanslots says the Magi were the first in the New Testament to use incense in the service of the Lord.
records.criticalEnglishAssessment: Matthew records frankincense among the Magi's gifts to the child Jesus. It does not establish a Christian incensing ritual, the origin of the Roman ceremony, or priority as the first people to incense at Christian worship.

The Lord Himself has sanctioned many of them by His own example. In the desert, when He was about to multiply the loaves in order to feed the hungry multitude, He first lifted His eyes to heaven ; who would doubt that He did the same when instituting this spiritual banquet, although it be not expressed in Holy Scripture? We need not observe, however, that this uplifting of the eyes to His Father and this thanksgiving do not imply that the Son is less than the Father ; t
records.lanslotsOriginalArgument: Lanslots argues that because Christ looked up at the multiplication of loaves he presumably raised his eyes at the Last Supper; he admits Scripture does not explicitly say this about the Last Supper.
records.criticalEnglishAssessment: Matthew 14:19 narrates the feeding of the multitude with uplifted eyes; Matthew 26:26 relates the Last Supper without a corresponding explicit eye-raising description. The 1962 priestly eyes-to-heaven rubric requires the Roman Missal as authority, not an invented Gospel event.

records.lanslotsOriginalArgument: Lanslots says Melchisedech offered bread and wine to God, blessed Abraham and distributed sanctified gifts to Abraham and his soldiers.
records.criticalEnglishAssessment: The biblical narrative states that Melchisedech brought forth bread and wine and was priest of the Most High; it does not detail a consecrated meal for Abraham's soldiers. How then can communion under one appearance be called a sacrilege? Those who do not receive sacramen- tally should endeavor
records.lanslotsOriginalArgument: Lanslots infers that because Luke mentions the breaking of bread and not a chalice, Christ gave sacramental Communion at Emmaus under one species.
records.criticalEnglishAssessment: Luke 24:30–31 describes Christ breaking bread and being recognized. It does not explicitly determine whether this was sacramental Communion or provide the complete distribution of species. Communion under one kind is nonetheless Catholic doctrine, with its proper basis in the Council of Trent, Session XXI, chapters I–III; a biblical argument from silence is not its proof.

invariants: The Bible text, its later theological reception and the 1897 author's conjectures are distinct evidential levels.
True Catholic teaching about sacrifice and Communion under one kind does not depend on unverifiable details of Emmaus or Melchisedech.
No nineteenth-century gesture allegory outranks the 1962 Ritus servandus.
